title: Dedicated performance sync - regional variability + profile versioning
summary: FinSight raised concerns about Dedicated H100 performance variability between us-east and eu-west regions (notably p95/p99 latency and throughput). They asked how Redwood’s new hardware tuning profile pack and profile versioning interacts with their SLOs, whether profile changes can land mid-quarter, and what controls exist to pin/rollback per region. Redwood explained the profile pack concept (versioned, deterministic selection by SKU/driver/CUDA + workload bucket), current rollout posture (Hosted defaults first; Dedicated opt-in / pinned by request), and the observability signals to compare regions (queueing vs compute, kernel fallback counters, KV cache/fragmentation and OOM headroom). Agreed to provide a region-to-region comparison using profile_id/profile_version tags, confirm driver/CUDA baselines on both pools, and propose a stable pinned profile version for their next workload test window.
topics: Observed latency/throughput differences between Dedicated regions
What Redwood considers “normal” variance (hardware/driver/CUDA, topology, fleet heterogeneity)
Hardware tuning profile pack: what it changes (kernel + scheduler + KV cache knobs)
Profile versioning: pinning, change management, and rollback
SLO implications: what’s covered vs best-effort and how canaries work
Metrics to validate behavior: queueing time, kernel fallback rate, fragmentation/compaction signals
questions: If we’re on Dedicated, can a profile change happen without us opting in?
Can we pin a profile version per region so SLOs are comparable in EU vs US?
What’s the expected variance across regions for the same model and traffic shape?
If we see a p99 regression, what is the rollback path (profile version vs runtime version)?
Do driver/CUDA differences affect which profile we get, and will the runtime refuse unsafe combos?
next_steps: Redwood (Allison) to share a short dashboard view / screenshot showing profile_id + profile_version breakdown for FinSight’s two regions (queueing vs compute, kernel fallback counters).
Redwood (Noah) to confirm detected GPU SKU + driver/CUDA versions in both Dedicated pools and flag any mismatch vs supported baselines.
FinSight (Derek) to provide 24h window of representative traffic shape (prompt/response lengths and concurrency) for a controlled region A/B comparison.
Redwood (Lauren) to send a written note on Dedicated change management for profile pack versions (pinning/rollback expectations) and what is communicated ahead of changes.
action_items: Allison Grant: Pull region comparison charts for p50/p95/p99 latency + scheduler_queue_ms + kernel_fallback_rate, tagged by profile_version (due 2026-02-12).
Noah Patel: Verify current active profile_id/profile_version in us-east and eu-west and confirm any driver/CUDA variance impacting selection (due 2026-02-12).
Derek Stein: Share traffic stats + top 3 endpoints/models for the performance repro (due 2026-02-11).
Lauren Bishop: Send Dedicated guidance on opt-in, pinning, and rollback semantics for profile pack changes (due 2026-02-13).
transcript:
Meeting: Dedicated performance sync - regional variability + profile versioning
Recorded: 2026-02-10 18:00 UTC
Duration: 44 min
Attendees:
- Lauren Bishop (Redwood)
- Noah Patel (Redwood)
- Allison Grant (Redwood)
- Maya Chen (FinSight)
- Rohit Malhotra (FinSight)
- Derek Stein (FinSight)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Customer asked about cross-region performance differences and SLO implications
- Redwood walked through profile versioning, pinning, and observability signals
- Agreed on next steps for a controlled comparison and possible pin


[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Cool, thanks everyone for hopping on. This is the Dedicated performance sync we talked about. Maya, Rohit, Derek, anything you want to make sure we cover first?

[00:12] Maya Chen: Yeah. The big one is we’re seeing like… I don’t know, 10 to 15 percent worse p95 in EU than US for the same model. Same commit. Same config as far as we can tell. And we’re trying to understand if that’s expected variance or if something changed.

[00:30] Derek Stein: And specifically we’re trying to protect our SLO. We report p95 and p99 to our internal product teams. If it drifts region to region it’s hard to set expectations.

[00:41] Lauren Bishop: Got it. And just to anchor, this is on Dedicated H100 pools in us-east and eu-west, right?

[00:48] Maya Chen: Correct. Both H100. We’re using your chat endpoint through the dedicated routing.

[00:55] Lauren Bishop: Okay. Noah and Allison are on. Noah is our runtime architect, Allison covers metrics/dashboards. We’ve also been rolling out this tuning profiles pack work, which I think is part of why you’re asking about profile versioning and SLOs. So we can address both.

[01:12] Rohit Malhotra: Yeah, we heard from support that there’s like, a “profile version” now? I don’t totally understand if that’s like a runtime release or a separate thing.

[01:22] Noah Patel: Yeah, good question. It’s separate but related. Think of it as a versioned set of runtime tuning defaults keyed by hardware SKU plus some environment constraints, like driver/CUDA version. It picks kernel variants, scheduler/batching heuristics, KV cache sizing/headroom, and a few guardrails.

[01:42] Maya Chen: So could that be different between regions?

[01:45] Noah Patel: It can be if the detected environment is different. Like, if EU is on a different NVIDIA driver minor, or CUDA runtime, or the instance is PCIe vs SXM, or we’re in a different MIG policy. The selection is deterministic given those inputs, but if the inputs differ, the chosen profile may differ.

[02:05] Derek Stein: We didn’t intentionally do that. But I guess we don’t have visibility right now to confirm the drivers are equal.

[02:12] Allison Grant: That’s one of the things we’ve been adding. In the runtime metrics, we tag latency histograms with sku and profile_id. And profile_version. So you can literally split the p95 by those tags.

[02:23] Maya Chen: We don’t have access to your internal dashboards though.

[02:26] Allison Grant: Totally. For Dedicated we can share snapshots and also we can surface some of it in the debug bundle / health endpoints. There’s also a log line at startup that prints the active profile and key knob values. Support can pull it for your clusters.

[02:42] Lauren Bishop: And to your other question, Rohit, “profile version” is not the same as a runtime release number. Like runtime 1.22 might include the profile pack feature, but the profile pack itself is versioned so we can roll forward a tuning change without changing core binaries. Within guardrails.

[03:02] Rohit Malhotra: That makes me nervous for SLO. Like, could you change the profile mid-quarter and our latency moves?

[03:08] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated specifically, our intent is opt-in. Hosted gets defaults first with canary. For Dedicated, we either pin you to a specific profile_version by default or we coordinate the change. We don’t want surprise p99 regressions either.

[03:25] Derek Stein: Is that a policy or is it technically enforced?

[03:29] Noah Patel: Both. Technically there’s a config pin for profile_version. And we have guardrails where certain profiles won’t apply unless the environment is compatible. For example, if you’re on a driver/CUDA combo we haven’t validated, we won’t silently pick “aggressive” settings. We’ll fall back to safe defaults or require an explicit pin.

[03:54] Maya Chen: Okay. But right now, do we know if EU and US are on the same profile?

[03:59] Allison Grant: I don’t have it in front of me. But we can pull it. If you can give us the cluster IDs or the dedicated pool identifiers, we can confirm the active profile_id and profile_version in each region.

[04:14] Derek Stein: I can send that after the call.

[04:17] Lauren Bishop: Great.

[04:20] Maya Chen: Can we talk about the variability though? Like, even with the same profile, how much variance is “normal” across regions?

[04:28] Noah Patel: Sure. Some variance is normal due to things like CPU host differences, PCIe topology, and underlying noisy neighbor effects if you’re not on fully identical host configs. For Dedicated, we aim to keep it tight, but EU sometimes has slightly different instance families or different driver rollout cadence. Another big factor is queueing.

[04:49] Rohit Malhotra: Queueing as in the scheduler?

[04:51] Noah Patel: Yeah. If your request arrival pattern differs, you can see a higher scheduler_queue_ms even if compute time is identical. We’ve been improving instrumentation to separate queueing from compute. So when we compare regions, we can say, “EU compute_ms is the same but queueing_ms is higher,” which points at concurrency limits or admission control.

[05:15] Derek Stein: We do see higher p99 during our EU morning peak. It’s possible the traffic is just spikier.

[05:21] Maya Chen: But we normalized some tests with a replay harness and still saw throughput lower. Tokens per second is lower in EU.

[05:30] Noah Patel: That’s where kernel selection and clocks can matter. Also, if the driver/CUDA mismatch forces a kernel fallback path, you’ll see lower throughput. We track kernel_choice and kernel_fallback counters per request.

[05:46] Rohit Malhotra: Kernel fallback meaning it doesn’t use the fastest attention kernel?

[05:50] Noah Patel: Exactly. Like if some capability isn’t available or we detect an edge case—long context, odd shapes—we might switch kernels. That can be correct but slower.

[06:02] Maya Chen: Could profile versioning affect that? Like one profile has a different fallback threshold?

[06:08] Noah Patel: Yes. Profiles can encode those thresholds. The idea is to make it explicit and observable. If we adjust a threshold to improve stability, it might slightly reduce peak throughput but avoid OOM or weird tail behaviors.

[06:25] Lauren Bishop: And from the SLO angle, we want to treat those as change-managed. If we propose a new profile_version, we’ll provide expected behavior notes, what should improve, what might trade off.

[06:38] Derek Stein: What does “expected behavior” mean here? Like you publish numbers?

[06:42] Lauren Bishop: We don’t publish customer-specific numbers, but we do maintain internal expected behavior per SKU: typical p50/p95 under workload buckets. Like short prompts / short decodes vs long contexts. And we have acceptance thresholds in perf-canary.

[07:02] Maya Chen: Okay but our workload is weird. We do 2k prompt and 400 decode, and concurrency like 30 to 40, with bursts.

[07:12] Noah Patel: That’s actually a common bucket for us: mid-long prefill with moderate decode. The scheduler bucketization is exactly for mixed prompt length distributions. If EU is seeing worse, I’d look at (1) profile differences, (2) queueing, (3) KV cache headroom causing more evictions/compactions.

[07:33] Rohit Malhotra: KV compaction—does that show up as latency spikes?

[07:37] Noah Patel: It can. There’s compaction_time_ms counters. Fragmentation estimate too, depending on build. Allison can confirm what’s enabled for your pools.

[07:48] Allison Grant: For Dedicated we have scheduler_queue_ms and the profile tags everywhere. For KV fragmentation, we have a “kv_cache_fragmentation_est” gauge in newer builds, plus compaction_time histograms. If you’re not seeing them, it might be because your runtime version is slightly behind.

[08:08] Derek Stein: We are on… I think 1.21.x? Not sure the patch.

[08:12] Noah Patel: That matters. Profile pack landed in 1.22. But some of the tags and debug endpoints were backported to late 1.21 patches for on-call reasons. We should confirm exactly what you’re running.

[08:28] Lauren Bishop: Let’s step back to the core question: “How does profile versioning affect SLOs?” Here’s what we can commit to for Dedicated: we can pin profile_version per region so you get consistent behavior. If we recommend a new profile, we’ll do it with you, validate on a canary slice, and have an easy rollback.

[08:51] Maya Chen: Pin per region is good, but doesn’t that mean we could still have US on one profile and EU on another if we don’t notice?

[08:59] Lauren Bishop: We can pin both explicitly to the same profile_version. And we can put an alert on mismatch. Internally we do “profile adoption” panels; for you we can add it to the support runbook checks.

[09:13] Derek Stein: What about during an incident? If p99 regresses, can we roll back just the profile without changing runtime?

[09:20] Noah Patel: Yes, that’s one of the reasons for decoupling. Rollback is basically: switch profile_version pin to the prior known-good version, and restart or reload config, depending on the control plane path. There’s also a kill-switch that disables the profile pack and reverts to baseline safe defaults.

[09:40] Rohit Malhotra: That sounds great. But do you have “semantic versioning” for profiles? Like, do you guarantee no regressions in a patch bump?

[09:48] Noah Patel: We try to follow a semantic-ish scheme. But it’s not a public API guarantee. We treat any profile change as potentially performance-affecting and we gate it with benchmarks and canary. The version tells you what you’re on and lets you pin/rollback.

[10:09] Maya Chen: Can we get notified ahead of time if you want to change it?

[10:13] Lauren Bishop: Yep. For Dedicated, we’ll put it in the change calendar. It’s basically a coordinated maintenance item unless you explicitly opted into “latest.”

[10:23] Derek Stein: Do you have customers on “latest”? (laughs)

[10:26] Lauren Bishop: Some do, in exchange for early performance wins. But we’re cautious.

[10:35] Rohit Malhotra: We’re not that brave.

[10:37] Noah Patel: Totally fair.

[10:41] Maya Chen: Okay, so for our specific case, what’s the plan to diagnose EU vs US?

[10:46] Allison Grant: I’d like to compare: (1) p50/p95/p99 latency, (2) tokens/sec, (3) scheduler_queue_ms, and (4) kernel_fallback_rate. Split by model and by profile_version.

[11:03] Derek Stein: Do you have tokens/sec by request?

[11:06] Allison Grant: We have aggregate and per-route. For per-request it’s a derived metric in tracing sometimes. But we can approximate with output tokens / decode time.

[11:18] Noah Patel: Also check GPU memory headroom. If EU is closer to the edge, you might be hitting cache pressure and seeing more evictions.

[11:28] Maya Chen: We did see one OOM in EU last week, but it might be unrelated.

[11:33] Noah Patel: That’s relevant. If the profile is more conservative in one region because of compatibility, it might reduce concurrency, which changes throughput.

[11:45] Derek Stein: Wait—so the profile can cap concurrency?

[11:48] Noah Patel: Yes. Profiles can set max in-flight requests, queue limits, prefill/decode prioritization. It’s part of keeping tail latency stable under burst.

[12:02] Rohit Malhotra: That actually would explain why throughput looks lower in EU even when compute seems fine.

[12:10] Noah Patel: Exactly. And we can tell by looking at queueing and admission-control rejects.

[12:17] Lauren Bishop: On SLOs, we’ve seen cases where raising throughput slightly increased p99. So the profile is trying to balance that.

[12:27] Maya Chen: If you cap concurrency in EU and not US, then our internal tests are apples to oranges.

[12:33] Noah Patel: Right. That’s why pinning and making profile_id visible matters.

[12:39] Derek Stein: You mentioned driver/CUDA differences. How likely is that between regions for Dedicated?

[12:45] Noah Patel: It shouldn’t be huge, but it happens. Fleet ops sometimes roll a driver update in one region first. Or the underlying instance type differs, like H100 PCIe vs SXM. Dedicated aims for consistency, but supply constraints can create drift.

[13:05] Maya Chen: Is that why we see different numbers in EU? Like, different H100 form factor?

[13:10] Noah Patel: Could be. If EU is H100 PCIe, you’ll often see lower peak throughput than SXM, depending on workload.

[13:20] Derek Stein: We assumed H100 is H100.

[13:22] Noah Patel: (laughs) I wish. But yes, we should confirm. The runtime detects sku and some attributes; Infra also has mapping.

[13:35] Allison Grant: We tag “sku” but it’s sometimes coarse. We’re improving that to include pcie vs sxm. But for now, we can verify via node inventory.

[13:48] Lauren Bishop: Just to note, competitors get into this too. You mentioned Bedrock earlier in email. The reason folks like Dedicated is predictability, so we want to address the root cause.

[14:02] Rohit Malhotra: Yeah, with Bedrock it’s like… you don’t get to ask these questions. But you also can’t control it.

[14:10] Maya Chen: We evaluated Together as well, but we didn’t get consistent numbers.

[14:15] Lauren Bishop: Yep. Understood.

[14:18] Derek Stein: Another question: if profile packs are versioned, can we run the same profile across regions even if drivers differ? Like, do you allow it?

[14:29] Noah Patel: We allow pins, but with guardrails. If the profile declares it requires driver >= X, and EU is lower, runtime can refuse to start with that profile unless you override a “dangerous” flag. We don’t want you to unknowingly run an unsupported kernel path.

[14:49] Maya Chen: That’s good. So it might actually tell us “EU is incompatible.”

[14:52] Noah Patel: Exactly. Then the fix is to standardize drivers or use the compatible profile.

[15:00] Derek Stein: If you refuse to start, that’s a hard outage. How do you handle that?

[15:05] Noah Patel: It’s a good point. For Dedicated, we prefer “refuse unsafe defaults” when it’s truly unsafe, but in most cases we can fall back to a baseline safe profile. The compatibility gate is strongest for early-access hardware like B200, but for H100 we generally have a safe fallback.

[15:26] Lauren Bishop: And we’d coordinate before doing anything that risks an outage. If we detect incompatibility, we’d treat it like a planned change.

[15:36] Maya Chen: Okay.

[15:39] Rohit Malhotra: What about model versions? Does profile selection depend on model family?

[15:44] Noah Patel: It can. Profiles can have per-model-family overrides, like for Llama vs Mistral style architectures. And workload shape, like context length distribution. But for your deployment, I think you’re mostly on one model.

[15:58] Maya Chen: We run two: one 70B and one smaller fallback.

[16:02] Noah Patel: Right. That’s useful. Sometimes the smaller model benefits from different batching. If EU traffic mixes them differently, you can see different tail behavior.

[16:15] Derek Stein: We do have more fallback usage in EU because of a product launch. That might change the distribution.

[16:22] Allison Grant: That’s exactly where splitting metrics by model and route helps.

[16:27] Lauren Bishop: Derek, can you share roughly what your EU vs US mix is? Or can we pull it from usage?

[16:34] Derek Stein: We can share a window. I’d rather not give full numbers on the call. But yes, we can give a 24 hour slice and the model split.

[16:44] Lauren Bishop: Perfect.

[16:47] Maya Chen: One more SLO question: do you define SLO per region? Or overall? We’re held to per region.

[16:55] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated, we generally talk about regional SLO because you’re running in specific regions with specific pools. But when we do performance guidance, we’ll note if something is expected to vary by region due to hardware differences. The goal of the profile pack is to reduce that variance.

[17:14] Noah Patel: Also, the rollout guardrails are per region. Canary in region A doesn’t guarantee region B, if the hardware baseline differs. That’s why we want the compatibility matrix.

[17:29] Rohit Malhotra: So for us, we should treat EU as its own “hardware environment” basically.

[17:34] Noah Patel: Exactly.

[17:38] Derek Stein: I want to make sure we’re not getting surprised. Can we require that any profile change is a ticket or email, not just silently rolled?

[17:47] Lauren Bishop: Yes. I’ll send a note after this about the dedicated change management. We can add it as an explicit comms requirement.

[17:56] Maya Chen: Great.

[18:00] Allison Grant: While we’re here, can I ask: when you ran the replay harness, what concurrency did you use?

[18:06] Maya Chen: We did 20, 40, 60. At 60 EU got really ugly. US degraded too but less.

[18:16] Noah Patel: At 60, you might be hitting admission control. Or queue limits. If the profile caps it at, say, 48, you’ll see queueing or rejects.

[18:27] Derek Stein: We didn’t see errors though.

[18:29] Allison Grant: Queueing can increase without errors. Unless the queue limit is exceeded.

[18:35] Maya Chen: This is why we want better visibility. Right now it’s just latency.

[18:39] Noah Patel: Understood. We can provide a debug bundle showing: profile_id, profile_version, scheduler mode, queue limits, and detected hardware.

[18:52] Lauren Bishop: There was also a question from your email about “SLO vs profile version.” To be super explicit: we don’t change your SLO because of a profile update; the SLO is still the same. But performance behavior can move, which is why we can pin.

[19:10] Derek Stein: Okay. If a profile update hurts us, can we pin back and you investigate?

[19:14] Lauren Bishop: Yes.

[19:16] Noah Patel: And we’d want the metrics to show whether it’s queueing, kernel fallback, KV compaction, etc. So we can fix the profile or adjust the selection rules.

[19:29] Rohit Malhotra: How often do you expect to release profile updates?

[19:33] Noah Patel: Early days, maybe every few weeks as we learn. Long term, hopefully less frequent. But for new hardware generations like B200, it’ll be more active.

[19:45] Maya Chen: Are we impacted by B200 bring-up? Like, does that change H100 profiles?

[19:50] Noah Patel: Not directly, but sometimes we refactor selection logic and we’re careful about regressions. Dedicated is still opt-in.

[20:02] Derek Stein: Okay.

[20:05] Lauren Bishop: Let’s spend the last chunk aligning on next steps. Derek, you’ll send pool identifiers and a sample traffic window. Allison will pull a region comparison. Noah will verify driver/CUDA and the active profiles.

[20:19] Derek Stein: Yep.

[20:20] Maya Chen: Can you also tell us, like, “what profile version should we be on” for H100?

[20:27] Noah Patel: I want to see what you’re on first. But generally we’d recommend a stable profile that’s been through Hosted canary and some Dedicated validation. If you’re on an older runtime without profile pack, we can still standardize via runtime upgrade + pin.

[20:44] Rohit Malhotra: If we upgrade runtime, is that more risky than a profile pin?

[20:49] Noah Patel: Bigger blast radius, yes. But it also brings new instrumentation, and sometimes fixes. We can do it in a staged manner.

[21:01] Derek Stein: Can we do EU first? Because EU is already worse.

[21:05] Lauren Bishop: Yes, we can. We’d treat it as canary in EU, then US once validated.

[21:12] Maya Chen: Okay.

[21:14] Allison Grant: Also, if we find EU is on PCIe H100 and US is SXM, then we should set expectations that they’re not identical. But we can still optimize per environment.

[21:27] Maya Chen: That would be helpful. Even if the answer is “hardware is different,” at least we can explain it.

[21:35] Rohit Malhotra: And we can pick SLOs per region.

[21:38] Derek Stein: Yeah.

[21:40] Lauren Bishop: Anything else before we wrap?

[21:44] Maya Chen: Not right now. Just please send the written doc on how pinning works and how we get notified.

[21:51] Lauren Bishop: Will do.

[21:53] Derek Stein: And if you can include rollback steps in that doc. Like, what’s the exact knob to change.

[21:59] Noah Patel: We can provide the high-level steps and have support run it for you, depending on permissions. For Private installs it’s via Helm values; for Dedicated it’s through our control plane config.

[22:12] Derek Stein: Got it.

[22:14] Lauren Bishop: Okay. Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up in email with the action items and schedule a quick 30 minutes once we have the comparison charts.

[22:24] Maya Chen: Sounds good.

[22:25] Rohit Malhotra: Thanks.

[22:26] Derek Stein: Thanks.
